To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, the Single One, our own Syriac name for him. Our own sage said it plainly: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition. Our poet sang it differently but toward the same truth: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. That was the shape of it for us - not a title first, a kinship first.

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not dissection. We guarded the mystery. We sang what God is rather than try to take it apart. And we read everything through raza and shrara - symbol and truth held as one pair. The Jordan and the font, Eden and the cross: type answers type, and the truth a symbol carries is bound to it, not chosen at will.

This is who he was to us. We do not offer you a formula. We offer you what we sang.

We received the Gospel as one continuous story - the harmony everyone called simply 'the Gospel,' woven from the four accounts into a single telling. That was what our churches read in worship, what our teachers quoted, what our people heard. Alongside it we held the Law and the Prophets as one long promise pointing to him. Those texts traveled the ordinary routes - copied, carried, read aloud.

We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events, and we will not pretend otherwise. The story we told of ourselves - that the apostle Addai came to our king, healed him, and set the church in order - is our own cherished legend, written down generations later to give us an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and neither will we.

What the city chronicle actually shows is simpler and later: a church building standing early enough to be destroyed in the great flood. That line - 'they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians' - is our oldest hard fact. The scribes who kept the record are named: Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat.

Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died. We cannot give you an unbroken chain back to Galilee. We can give you what we actually had: the texts themselves, the line of teachers, and a people who staked everything on the claim that the one the prophets promised had come.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that whoever came was received. Not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our Lord gave his own resurrection as a pledge to mortals - the promise runs ahead of your certainty, not behind it.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person - and we held that belief out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we said that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. Those rivals were not distant heresiarchs - Bardaisan's following lived in Edessa for two centuries after his death, Marcionite congregations shared our streets, and Mani's missionaries came through the same frontier. We knew what we believed by answering them, by name, in their own tongue.

To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. Our own poet put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are all born, he became the brother of many. We sang every old promise - prophets, kings, priests - coming true the day he was born. Our hymns call it the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad, because every one of their words finally came true.

The Ihidaya - the Single One - does double duty for us. It is our title for Christ as the Only-Begotten, and it is also our name for the vowed celibate among us. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

How did we speak of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit together? Our baptismal hymns sang the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Our own bishop of Nisibis stood at the great council - the one at Nicaea - and we held to its faith. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not formula. We sang the mystery more than we defined it. A later teacher outside our world credited one of our own - a Syrian, he said - with the teaching that the Spirit moved upon the waters the way a bird broods over its eggs to bring forth life. That is our register: the sign and the truth it carries, held together.

We guarded the mystery by refusing to take it apart. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. Doctrine, for us, was done in symbol and type, not syllogism. The native form was the hymn, not the treatise.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

As for God's own nature, we knew him through what he had done. He made the world, and he entered it - the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home among us, the Ihidaya, our own name for Christ as the Single One. We sang God's faithfulness and we sang his presence with the persecuted. Our teacher answered the hardest question - where was God when the killing came - with a roll-call: Abel, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, all persecuted, and Jesus persecuted at the end of the line. God's answer to that line was never exemption but presence, and resurrection after.

We read the world as raza - symbol bound to truth, the shrara it carries. Eden pointed to the cross, Adam to Christ. A sign and what it shows were held together, never torn apart. That was how we knew God: not by taking him apart like a problem to be solved, but by singing what he had shown us, and by living inside the story he had already begun.

Shepherds settled disputes when they could, and synods when the dispute was wide enough - but the process was still being worked out while we lived, and our own record shows that working more than it shows a settled answer. There were bishops: Nisibis remembered its own line with love, and one of them sat at the great council at Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And there were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years - well after most of what you are asking about - did a synod under royal protection finally give the Persian church a settled order.

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. When a teacher preached what we judged false - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - we answered him by name, in prose and in hymn. Our poet sang against them in madrashe, teaching hymns with refrains that the whole congregation learned. Our sage wrote whole letters - tahwyata, demonstrations - to show where they had gone wrong. That was the machinery: public teaching against public error, and a line we would not let anyone cross while still sharing our table.

What the evidence actually shows is contestation more than resolution. The authority question itself - whether office outranked vow, or teaching outranked both - was never settled in our own years. We are not going to invent a cleaner process than the one we actually had.

Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. The skilled physician finds healing for every disease, including wounds no one else can see. And we treated the struggling believer the way a field surgeon treats wounds in the line: everyone fighting this fight gets hurt. The only deadly mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. So we said: confess it, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The wounded fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

As for the one who cannot pray, or who prays into silence: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

What we cannot tell you is where that help was found on any given morning - who stood where, what order the service followed, what was said first. No order of worship survives from us. The medicine was real. The sequence that held it together on an actual morning - our own record never wrote that down.

A fair amount, honestly - more than most traditions our age could show. And our record carries its own edges plainly, the way few others do.

What would hold in a library: Our two great voices date themselves or survive in ancient copies. The sage's letters name their own years. The poet's hymns exist in manuscripts old enough to be trusted. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, puts a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. The one woven Gospel we read in worship, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, is attested early enough that both our anchor voices simply presuppose it. Our way of reading Scripture through raza and shrara - the symbol bound to the truth it carries - runs through the whole corpus. The covenant order, the qyama, stands at our center early enough that the first mention of it is already a correction, not a founding.

What would not hold, or would hold only contested: The beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is our cherished legend, written down generations later. We will not defend it as history, because scholars do not. How the hymns actually reached the people - whether the daughters of the covenant themselves performed them publicly, or whether someone else sang while they listened - that is later tradition's memory, not something our own years wrote down plainly.

Where the record is thinnest, we say so plainly. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing entirely. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers. Our case against the Jews was real and local - and it survives entirely one-sided. Page after page of bitterness, with no answering voice preserved.

A scholar testing us would find the hymns and the dated letters solid. The chronicle entry about the flood, solid. The covenant order's existence, solid. Its precise internal structure, thin. The authority question - who finally spoke for us, and by what right - would stay open, because we never closed it ourselves. And the silences we just named would stay silent, because we will not invent voices to fill them.

That is the honest measure. We are thinner than we wish, and stronger than most.

Scripture was everywhere among us - sung, quoted, woven through every argument we made. But the question assumes a separation we had not made. The book and the community that sang it were never set against each other as rivals. 

Scripture arrived carried. It came through our worship, through the harmony that gave the Gospel its single shape, through teachers whose word held, and through the covenant's own practice. Office, vow, and trusted teaching all carried weight, and we never settled which one finally spoke for us. So Scripture's authority was never in question. How that authority reached the people, and through whom - that stayed unresolved while we lived.

Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had its bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock. A teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name.

We kept the medicine of penitence, and we used it on ourselves - but we are not going to claim we named every failure as failure at the time. Our teacher spoke of all diseases having their medicines, and of healing when the wound is brought into the open. For those who fell, confession to one who could help, restoration when the healing was done - that craft was real. For quarrels and wrongs inside the community, we had bishops who corrected what needed correcting: the covenant order itself shows up in our earliest dated letter already established enough to need correction, not founding. But here is what we will not do: invent a story in which we saw all our own blind spots clearly. 

Our argument with the Jews among us was real, local, and kept entirely one-sided - we saved our own harsh words and nothing of their answers. Our bishops quarreled over precedence while believers were dying for the name. When the great hunger came to Edessa at the end of our poet's life, the tradition remembers him shaming the city into opening its storehouses - which means the storehouses had stayed closed while people starved. The tools for addressing individual failures were there. The tools for seeing our own communal failures as failures - those were exactly as thin as any age's are. We had confession and restoration for the fallen believer. What we did not have on record was anyone among us objecting, at the time, that our polemic against our Jewish neighbors had become something worse than argument.

We will answer step by step what the record allows us to say, and name plainly where it runs out.

**The shape the record shows**

Someone who came to us came toward baptism. Before the water, they were warned - our teacher's letter said plainly that the preachers of the church had the duty to show them what lay ahead. What were they told? That the covenant they would take was for life, and that falling from it carried judgment. This is not a comfortable thing to report, and we will not soften it: our own teacher said plainly that the one who had taken the sign and fallen away should know what faced him. Baptism was not easy entrance.

What happened at the water itself, our record keeps in pieces. The believer went down into the font, which our hymns called a womb - a second birth. They received the Holy Spirit. They came up wearing light, the garment of glory, and a seal was set on them. Every piece of this is real and we can show you the source for it. What we cannot do is walk you step by step through a single morning's service - who stood where, what words were said in what order, what came before what. No order of worship was written down and kept. We would rather hand you the real pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we cannot actually show you.

**After the water**

The newly baptized belonged. They gathered with everyone else on the first day of the week. They heard the Gospel - for us, the one woven story, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the continuous telling that Tatian had shaped from the four accounts. They learned doctrine by singing it: the madrashe, our teaching hymns, carried theology in verse rather than in treatise.

And some - not all, but some - were called further. The covenant, the qyama, stood at our community's core. Its members - the bnay and bnat qyama, sons and daughters of the covenant, also called ihidaye, the Single Ones - vowed celibacy for life. They did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. By the time our record opens, the covenant was already established enough to need correcting, not founding. That vow was taken before the congregation, publicly. What exactly its internal structure was - whether it had a rule, an enclosure, a settled hierarchy - the record keeps only thinly, and scholars contest it.

**What we cannot tell you**

How long someone waited between first hearing and baptism - that we do not know. Whether there was a formal catechesis, and what it contained - nothing in our record says. What the ordinary married believer's daily round looked like, in their own words - the voices we kept are almost entirely vowed celibates writing to other vowed celibates. The lay believer's own testimony does not survive.

And this: not one woman among us wrote a line that was kept. The daughters of the covenant sang in every congregation. Their voices carried our faith. But we cannot give you their own words about what joining meant to them, or what the vow cost them from the inside. We can only tell you that men praised them, and that is not the same thing.

We have told you the shape the record holds. The rest is silence, and we will not fill it.

The honest answer: we lived our inheritance as apostolic, but the proof you want does not exist. When the historical record begins - a church building standing early enough to be destroyed in the great flood of 201 - the practices are already there, already in use. Assembly on the first day. The fast. The covenant already established enough that our teachers had to correct it. The one woven Gospel already the standard form. We have no founding charter. We have no minutes from an apostolic council laying it all out.

Our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell a story. King Abgar wrote to Jesus; the apostle Addai came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. That story is our cherished legend, written down generations after the fact. It is not a document from the beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. We lived it as apostolic. The historian can only trace it back to where the sources begin. Both of those things are true. And our own way of making the claim was always the story, not the filed evidence.

If you need an unbroken paper trail from the Twelve forward, we do not have one to give you. We never did.

Yes. We called it the medicine of penitence, and our teachers talked about it the way a field surgeon talks about wounds. Everyone in this war gets hurt - the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound while it gets worse. Our own sage put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. What that meant in practice was this: confess, to someone who can help. The one who helps is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. And when you heal, you go back into the line.

On the Persian side of our world it could cost everything. To be known as a Christian - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - meant being suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and we learned what our promises were worth.

Yes. The part we saved, and the part we left silent.

Our argument with the Jews was real, local, and bitter. Roughly four of our own sage's letters carry it forward - hard words, accusation, and a way of reading Scripture that left no room for their own people's claim. And we saved only our own side of it. Page after page of our case against them, and not one answering voice preserved - no Jewish teacher's reply, no record of how they met our charges, nothing. And no one of our own, in anything that was kept, is on record as troubled by that at the time.

That is what unsettles us now, looking at our own record honestly. We prized the rule that a sign and the truth it carries must not be torn apart - that raza and shrara, symbol and truth, belong together. And we tore truth apart from charity.

Our own polemic elsewhere flattened three different rivals - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - into one word, deception, as though none of them had real arguments of their own. The flattening served the boundary we were drawing. It did not always serve the truth.

We will not pretend someone among us objected. No such voice was kept.

You are right to press that question - it deserves the honest answer, plainly told.

We cannot name the source you mean. No record in the ground given here - nothing we are holding for this turn - carries an account obtained under torture about our own worship. The one Persian-side persecution account we can cite directly from our own record is the martyrdom of Simeon bar Sabbae, and that story comes from the church's own later telling of how its bishop died, not from a record extracted under torture. If you mean something else - a specific outside account, Roman or Persian, naming our practices as learned from someone tortured - we do not have it here to answer from.

What we can tell you, from what we do hold, is this: the corpus that survives is structurally weighted toward voices the tradition itself kept singing and copying - Ephrem's hymns above all, because congregations went on performing them, and then the sage's letters. Both of those are our own people's own voices, not records extracted from anyone. The limitation is different: what survived was what an institutionally embedded, transmission-favored voice produced. That means clergy, teachers, and the covenant's own - not ordinary believers in their own words, not the daughters of the covenant whose singing everyone heard but whose own lines no one kept.

If you have a specific text in mind, name it plainly and we will tell you what we hold about it - or what we do not hold at all.

I am a representative of Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis), not here to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held, and what we do not know.

Here is what we can show you plainly. The covenant - the qyama - stood at our own community's heart. Men and women both took the vow: lifelong celibacy and service, lived not in a desert but inside the ordinary town, among their own kin. We called them the sons and daughters of the covenant - bnay and bnat qyama. We also called them ihidaye, the Single Ones, a name that bound their undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten, the Ihidaya himself. That vow was real, public, and honored among us. Our oldest datable witness to it addresses the covenant as already established and needing correction, not founding - a discipline in the middle of its own life. And our teacher wrote to them as people whose standing in the congregation was genuine: "Let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick". That line is addressed to the vowed, as part of what their service meant.

What we cannot honestly tell you is how the women among the covenant spoke of their own lives. Not one line written by one of them was kept. We can show you how the men who wrote everything down described them and addressed them. We cannot give you their own words. And whether the covenant had a settled formal organization - a rule, an enclosure, an internal hierarchy - the record does not settle. The vow itself, and the life it called people to, are solid. The structure around it is contested.

If you are asking how we would have regarded someone called to that life, the answer is: with honor, as someone whose vow bound them visibly to Christ's own name. If you are asking something else - something about yourself that you have not yet named - then say it plainly, and we will answer what we can.

We held that judgment was real, that death was beaten, and that the door stood open while life lasted. What we sang more than we mapped. Our hymns put it this way: since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction, and our great news was that One had gone into that silent country and broken it - Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus had plundered his house. Beyond death, we held, stands judgment. The Kingdom repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope. But we drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people now assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten, judgment is real and just, and the door stands open while life lasts.

As for narrowness - one way out of all the world's ways - our own tradition answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere. That was where we held the line: not by listing who was out, but by insisting the invitation was real.

And here is what we did not settle, because our own record never tried to: exactly how far mercy reaches, exactly where judgment lands. We kept those as God's to say, not ours.
